title: Genome intuition, made legible
subtitle: Pharma R&D · Genomics
summary: A research team had genomic insight locked in notebooks and ad-hoc scripts — intuition that never reached the shared system. We co-architected a genome browser and annotation workflow with embedded scientists, preserving how researchers actually reason about variants.
problem: A research team had genomic insight locked in notebooks and ad-hoc scripts — intuition that never reached the shared system.
intervention: We co-architected a genome browser and annotation workflow with embedded scientists, preserving how researchers actually reason about variants.
outcome: Scientists stopped exporting to desktop tools; decision-ready views shipped inside the platform.
challenge: Turn tacit genomic reasoning into software that scientists would actually use — without forcing them into a workflow that erased how they think about variants.
whatWeDid: Mapped how scientists actually navigate variants across notebooks, scripts, and tribal knowledge
Co-architected a genome browser and annotation workflow with embedded domain scientists
Preserved researcher agency in the interface instead of flattening intuition into rigid forms
Shipped decision-ready views inside the platform so insight no longer lived only on desktops

title: Automation without losing the bench
subtitle: Biotech · Lab automation
summary: Robotic synthesis runs were technically correct but opaque — operators couldn't intervene when the science drifted. We designed human-in-the-loop controls and exception surfaces on top of existing automation, without stripping agency from the bench.
problem: Robotic synthesis runs were technically correct but opaque — operators couldn't intervene when the science drifted.
intervention: Human-in-the-loop controls and exception surfaces on top of existing automation, without stripping agency from the bench.
outcome: Fewer silent failures; operators recovered runs that previously became scrap.
challenge: Keep robotic synthesis reliable while giving operators a real way to intervene when science drifts — without ripping out the automation already in place.
whatWeDid: Audited where silent failures hid inside otherwise “correct” robotic runs
Designed human-in-the-loop controls and exception surfaces on existing automation
Kept bench operators in the decision loop instead of automating agency away
Reduced scrap by making recoverable drifts visible early enough to act

title: The $38k wrong question
subtitle: Clinical · Reporting
summary: A report builder was months into build. Scientists still printed batch results and taped them to the bench. One week of user research reframed the ask before more code shipped — the real need was print-at-point-of-use.
problem: A report builder was months into build. Scientists still printed batch results and taped them to the bench.
intervention: One week of user research reframed the ask before more code shipped — the real need was print-at-point-of-use.
outcome: The wrong question cost $38,000. The right one was a print button.
challenge: Stop an expensive build from answering the wrong question — scientists needed results at the bench, not another report builder.
whatWeDid: Ran one week of user research before more engineering spend
Found the real workflow: print batch results and tape them next to physical samples
Reframed the product ask from “better report UX” to print-at-point-of-use
Replaced months of wrong-direction work with a fix that matched how the lab actually operates
